utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could I ask the Court officer to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-82-T, The Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've already had the appearances of counsel. I notice no change, so we won't go through that again. The case was listed today to commence hearing the evidence in the case. Before that, I understand counsel have one or two procedural matters. These will need to be dealt with quite quickly. We don't want to lose time unnecessarily. And just before we proceed to those, may I check firstly with Mr. Boskoski, whether he can hear a translation in his language. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Tarculovski. THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. From now on, the Chamber will assume that you are hearing a translation in your language. If ever you are not, please either signal to your counsel or stand up and let the Chamber know. Thank you. Now, there are matters which counsel wish to raise. The first concerns an intended Prosecution witness who was to be called later, but the Prosecution now wish to bring him forward in their list, I understand, to the 21st of May because he has planned to be across the Atlantic for some time from a few days after the 21st. Can I indicate to counsel that the Chamber is aware that that would create practical problems in the preparation of the Defence. Certain confidential ex parte procedural orders have been made by the Chamber which relate to this witness, and there would simply not be sufficient time for the Defence to assess and assimilate material which it is anticipated will be provided to them from various sources pursuant to those orders if the witness is to be called by the 21st of May. Therefore, Mr. Saxon, the answer is, I'm afraid, "No" to the 21st of May. It would not be fair to the Defence. The question then becomes: When, at a later time, it will be convenient? And it may well mean that it will be necessary to bring the witness back temporarily from wherever he is to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. May we move into private session briefly, please, since I may discuss some matters that relate to a personal nature for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I simply wanted to explain to the Trial Chamber, if it hasn't been understood previously, that the Prosecution's concern with respect to this witness is simply that as it is intended that the Prosecution's case will be relatively short, then the Prosecution was concerned that the Prosecution's case would be over before the witness was back on this continent, and so that -- therein has lied the difficulty, and we will do our best to propose the solution that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can deal with the matter one of two ways, Mr. Saxon; either slow down, not to the point where we notice it, and drag out your case, or you can proceed as you are proposing. Now, I think you would find that if you tried to slow down, we would notice it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution takes that fully on board, Your Honour, and we will not try to slow down. We will do our best to stay with our schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We all appreciate it's important to deal with the case as quickly and as fairly as possible. Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yeah, very briefly on this matter, Your Honour, if I may. The Defence is quite sympathetic, I have to say, to the travel arrangements of this particular witness. However, we believe that VWS could assist this particular witness perhaps in obtaining the visa which he would need to come back to this continent and, if necessary, go back to this other place. The Defence is quite concerned by the request of the Prosecution for the videolink. We believe it's an important witness, and we believe that it's a witness that must be seen in person to assess his reliability. The other concern which we have, which is the one that you've highlighted earlier on, is certainly one of timing, Your Honour. There is a number of pending matters that we are expecting, material which we expect to receive and to review. There is also another matter which I would bring to the attention of the Chamber at this stage, and it's an ongoing discussion with the Prosecution about certain information which do relate to this witness. We've received a letter early this morning in relation to this matter. Unfortunately, we believe that the response is unresponsive at this stage, so we will have to pursue this matter further. And this may again impact on not only the timing of calling of this witness, but perhaps even on the admissibility of his evidence. So we will endeavour to go as fast as possible with the Prosecution and hopefully to find a solution, but we believe that at this stage the fairest solution to the Defence, in any case, would be for this witness to be called later and in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mettraux. Now, we've taken nearly ten minutes over the first matter, and I have a note of several matters. We want to be rid of them all by a quarter to 3.00 and move into evidence, so counsel will need to be quicker. The next matter is, I think, again by the Boskoski Defence, is it, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We've been very demanding with your patience today, and I'll try to be very quick. It relates to the consolidation process of statements by the Prosecution, and I think, to save time, we will make a formal response to the Prosecution applications in writing. At this stage, all we would like to point out to Your Honour is the fact that the consolidation process seems to have been more than what Your Honour ordered. We understood Your Honour's order as ordering the Prosecution to merely avoid repetitions in the statements and to produce one statement which would encompass all of the evidence of that witness without anything else. We understood it to be merely a stylistic exercise of removing repetitions. We're quite concerned that we have identified a number of amendments, of withdrawals, of deletions, or of simply of a succession of evidence which may have the effect of neutralising, for example, contradictions between statements. I won't go into identifying them at this stage because we don't have the time, but what has happened in a number of statements is that successive shades of evidence, if you want, have been placed one after the other, thereby suggesting that the witness from the beginning gave that evidence, which is not the case. The evidence evolved, which may or may not be relevant to Your Honour and to the Defence, but what we would wish is to have a purely neutral exercise of consolidation. At this stage, we're quite concerned that the exercise has been more confusing than anything else. There again, we've asked the Prosecution to provide us with a copy of those statements which would highlight all deletions and all additions, if any, have been made in the statements, as some have been made so that it would facilitate the response of the Defence, and at this stage we could decide whether to challenge the admission of the statements themselves. However, at this stage, I would also like to respond to generally some assertions which are made, because they concern some witnesses which will come this week. The Prosecution suggests that the addendum are an integral part of the consolidated statement. Well, that's contrary to Your Honour's order. Another thing of concern to us are the numbers of addendum and corrigendum which now come our way, and we're quite concerned about the status of the evidence which has already been admitted, to the extent that the evidence now added to the statement is contrary to the original one. Which one is reliable? The original statement which has been admitted, the new one? And we don't even know how this evidence will be led now. There's also another matter that I would like to highlight. It concerns the documents. The Prosecution has told us now that they will not seek to tender the comments of the witness in relation to particular exhibits; however, that they reserve their right, as we understood it, at a later stage. Well, it's the Defence position this would be quite incorrect. If the Prosecution intends to use the evidence of that witness in relation to particular documents, they have the duty to do it now. If they seek later to tender those exhibits and to use that statement in one way or another as an attachment, the Defence will not be able to cross-examine on those. And unless it's being done in chief, we will not or we might not examine the witness on those exhibits. So if the Prosecution intends to ever tender these comments or this evidence of the proposed witness in relation to that document, we believe it should be done at this stage. As I pointed out, I will stop now, Your Honour, but we will respond in writing to highlight perhaps for the Chamber some of the difficulties which we have with those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, to the best of my knowledge, the Prosecution has not received a request from the Defence to provide copies of these prior statements with highlighted deletions, so perhaps the Defence counsel could check on whether that has actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It was sent on the 1st of May, Mr. Saxon. We will send it again, Your Honour, so that it can accelerate things today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution produced these consolidated statements pursuant to the written decisions and instructions of the Trial Chamber and pursuant to the presiding Judge's instructions from the pre-trial conference that was held on the 12th of April, where His Honour Judge Parker noted that addendums -- additional information or corrections that come up during proofing need also be addressed, and so that is simply what we did. And it's the Prosecution's position that the 92 ter package, if I may, would not be complete without the consolidated statement and additional information that was provided during the proofing process. And so that's why we tried to do it this way, to try to provide the Defence with as much information as possible in as advanced time as much as possible. And, thirdly, we will use the exhibits -- certain exhibits with accused -- excuse me, with Prosecution witnesses who are testifying underneath rule 92 ter, and we will do this viva voce, so there shouldn't be any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see that there is no wish of Mr. Apostolski to be heard at this time. The Chamber would make a few very brief comments in the hope that it may clear some of the issues in the minds of counsel. First, the order of the Chamber with respect to those witnesses whose evidence is to be led in chief with the use of a Rule 93 ter statement, there being before the Chamber and the parties more than one statement from that witness, the Chamber's order was that the Prosecution should consolidate the several statements so that one statement was produced which became the 93 ter statement -- 92 ter, I beg your pardon, deleting unnecessary repetition, because there was quite a deal of repetition as one went from one statement to another of the same witness. Now, that becomes then the consolidated statement, the statement which will be received as the statement of the witness when the witness is called here. A second and distinct issue is one that is quite usual and typical; a witness, when asked to consider past statements made a year or two or more ago, will often note matters which they now have a different view about or note matters they believe were not correctly recorded originally, note matters which they now consider to have been omitted or note matters which are there which they think should not be there. In other words, they want to make some changes to previous written statements. There is no objection to them making changes. The effect of change may be that there is an embarrassment to Defence in cross-examining. If that should arise, there may be a need for some allowance of time to allow the Defence to consider the change before cross-examining on that issue. Importantly, no statement of any of those witnesses is yet in evidence. The fact that they were tendered under 92 bis or ter, they have not been admitted. They will only be admitted when the witness comes here, and if the witness, when he comes here or she comes here, says, "Well, this is my statement, I believe this evidence to be entirely correct except that on page 2, line whatever, this needs to be changed, and on page 3, some other matter needs to be changed," that will be part of the evidence of the witness given here, with those changes. The procedural orders of the Chamber seek to ensure that the Defence will have been aware of what the witness originally said in the original statement, in each of more than one original statements, and what the witness now wants to say about a matter, so that Defence will have available all of the progressive changes, if there are any, of a witness so that the Defence is in a position to cross-examine about those changes if the Defence considers them to be material. And we seek, as a matter of fairness, to try and ensure that the Defence has notice of each of those versions and any changes that are wanted to be made here at the moment the witness gives evidence. There is a third and, again, distinct matter. The Prosecution may want to put to a witness a particular exhibit or a number of exhibits to have the witness's comments or observations about the exhibit or some matter concerned with the exhibit. That is a perfectly normal and proper part of the evidence of the witness, as the evidence-in-chief is given. It needs normally to be given during -- or done during the evidence-in-chief of the witness, so that when the Defence comes to cross-examine, it will already be known, the full scope of that witness's evidence. So there should not be a problem there. What can occur occasionally is that something raised in cross-examination introduces some new issue about which the Prosecution, in their re-examination, need to put to the witness some further exhibit. Now, that is proper where it arises out of the cross-examination by one or other Defence counsel. Apart from that, the Prosecution should lead from the witness, when the witness comes to give evidence-in-chief, all the evidence they seek from that witness, including any observations about exhibits that they want that witness to give. Now, I hope that those comments will help counsel understand the process a little more clearly as we proceed. Now, is there a further matter, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, two very briefly, Your Honour. First, we're grateful for the indications. We will respond according to your clarifications, Your Honour. The other two matters pertains to the Defence ability to prepare, and very briefly, for the record, the first one concerns the issue of translations of Defence documents. We've had a number of communications with CLSS where they've indicated to us that they would wish us to deprioritise, as it goes, a number of documents. It's very difficult for us to do that at this stage, not knowing which witness, apart from the first 15, will come. We've been very willing and we've attempted to be as cooperative as we could with CLSS, but I just wish to indicate at this stage that there seems to be some problem with the speed at which the documents are translated, and I insist to point out that we are not blaming CLSS. They are working with finite resources at this stage, and we have no reason to believe that they work less than -- as hard as and as fast as they can, but we are quite concerned at this stage that perhaps the registry should be notified of that fact to see whether any further resources could be given to CLSS as far as Macedonian translations are concerned. The last matter finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I make an observation briefly on that before we pass from it? I have been aware and the Chamber has been very interested in efforts to provide adequate translation of written material, as well as adequate interpretations of oral submissions and evidence which we are now commencing on into Macedonia. This is the first trial in this Tribunal which has involved the Macedonian language. It has been necessary to recruit people to undertake this new role, and it has been very difficult to obtain people with suitable experience because there appears to be a growing demand in a number of parts of Europe and elsewhere in the world for people with this interpretive and translation skill. The Macedonian speakers can be assured that if law isn't going well, they can turn to interpretation, it would appear. The effect is that the -- it has not been possible to engage as much resource as would have been ideal. It's understood that the resources which have been found of a suitable quality will be adequate, but at the start of a trial like this, when both the Prosecution and the Defence are providing very large quantities of written material and hoping to have almost immediate translations, physically the task is simply not possible. So anything that can be done by counsel to identify the documents that are going to be needed first or most importantly would assist in the process of identifying the documents to be translated first. Otherwise, it's simply a matter of the supply and demand. It will simply take time, and it will not be possible to produce translations of everything immediately. Now, the Chamber has this under observation and will be watching progress, both in the areas of discovery, in the areas of Defence obtaining of further materials, which have been the subject of confidential orders, and in this matter of translations. As I did mention perhaps obscurely when we were last together and opening statements were made, the Chamber is watching the progress and has in mind that perhaps by the end of this first month, it may be necessary to have yet a further few days' break to assist in the process of everything catching up. We will watch that, and it may be that the last couple of days of May and the first couple of days of June could be a convenient time to enable people who are under great pressure, both counsel here and the translation and other services, to catch up with the demands that are there. So just be aware that we're looking to that possibility, but as we judge the witnesses that are first being called, there should not be major difficulties over the matters we are speaking about. They will become most important with later witnesses in the Prosecution case. So we'd hope to be able to sit at least for three weeks without any problem, maybe then with just -- I mention those particular dates because there is a public holiday at the end of the month, and it may be in that week we could add to the public holiday and have a few more days' break to enable everybody to be more in command of all the materials. The Chamber is well aware that it is a very difficult time at the commencement of a case to get everything in order that's needed both for Prosecution and Defence, and we will keep that matter under observation. Now, Mr. Mettraux, your very last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would be grateful for this indication as well, Your Honour, about that timing. The last matter is -- relates to the EDS. We've been told by the Prosecution on a number of occasions that the EDS system, the uploading into the EDS, would be finalised by early March, then April, a number of dates were mentioned. At this stage, the EDS is not yet fully uploaded. I'm told that there is approximately 20 batches that are outstanding and missing from the EDS. Again, we don't wish to criticise the Prosecution at this stage. I mean, they've had their loads -- loads of work to do as well, but we are very concerned that this could impede our ability to prepare. And, hopefully, this week it would be possible for the Prosecution to finalise the uploading of the missing batches. As I said, we believe there are 20 missing. We will give an indication to the Prosecution of those batches which we think are missing, but we really hope that the full uploading of the material can be done and finalised by the end of this week so as to ensure that we are able to fully prepare over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. I think that's another one to add into that list of all the -- the little things that are under great strain at the moment, and the sooner they can be got into place, the easier it will be for all people. Mr. Saxon, you had a matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Actually, to respond, first of all, to my colleague, I can inform the Chamber that to the best of my knowledge, batches 23 to 33 will be available on the EDS system for counsel to use by the close of business today. With regard to other so-called Prosecution disclosure batches, it takes, I'm told by the technical people that work with the Office of the Prosecutor to operate the EDS, it takes about a week for -- after a request is made to put something on the system, for that material to actually arrive and be accessible on the system. That is simply because there are a number of trials operating at once and a great deal of disclosure going on. But we will certainly endeavour and I will speak again to the technical people to make sure that this work is done as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Saxon. Now, that concludes Boskoski Defence. Is there any matter which the Tarculovski Defence needs to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to thank you for your intervention with regards to fast completion of translations, and I wish to stress that after the intervention by the Trial Chamber, the translations are actually arriving faster. So I think that they will be completed in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tarculovski -- I beg your pardon, Mr. Apostolski. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but the Prosecution has one matter which it believes will affect many of the early witnesses, and it's simply the issue of the ability to ask leading questions during direct examination. The Prosecution has spoken with Defence counsel for both accused about this matter, and there is a certain agreement which hopefully I can explain clearly. It's simply this: The parties have agreed that when a witness begins his or her testimony, the Prosecution may use leading questions to establish facts such as the witness's name and identity, where the witness is from, et cetera, et cetera, to save time. Your Honour, where there is perhaps less of a meeting of the minds, and I seek some guidance from the Trial Chamber, is certain procedural and factual questions that must be addressed with either 92 ter or 92 bis witnesses, questions about whether, "Did you provide one or more statements over the years to members of the Office of the Prosecutor?", "Is the contents of your statement true and correct," et cetera, et cetera. And I would like to ask some guidance -- for some guidance from the Bench, respectfully, if the Bench will also allow the Prosecution to use leading questions to establish these fundamental elements for the admission of 92 bis statements or 92 ter written statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, the description "leading questions" is perhaps provocative and slightly misleading. Those familiar with adversarial examination, as you are, will know that with any witness, both Prosecution and Defence, it is often necessary to direct the attention of the witness to a particular subject matter about which questions are then going to be asked which are material to the issues in the case. Those introductory questions or observations, which are merely bringing the witness to a subject matter, are perfectly proper and save much time. But what is to be avoided is questioning which suggests to the witness the answer desired when the witness is dealing with any of the issues that are material in the case and which are the subject of dispute. I'm sure that as we find our way through the first few witnesses, those delineations will become a little more clear to counsel, and they will become familiar and at ease with how far they may go by way of introductory comment directing a witness to a particular subject matter. Was that enough to help you for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We didn't manage it in the half hour, but we have managed it in my -- within my fallback position. We've done it in 40 minutes. I gave ourselves an absolute limit of three-quarters of an hour. So thank you very much for your cooperation there. If it would be practical now to bring in the first witness, please, Mr. Court Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, Ms. Motoike will call the first witness and lead the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon. The Prosecution at this time would call Mrs. Zenep Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Motoike. The Court Officer is already going to the room where the witness is waiting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to this witness, I believe the Prosecution sent an e-mail to the Chamber advising the Chamber and the court staff about her need to have the declaration read to her, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Zenep.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you simply to acknowledge at the end. Do you solemnly declare that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you please sit down. Now, the process now is that Ms. Motoike will be asking some questions of you. I think you have met her already. And if you would listen to her and respond to her questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Is your legal name Zenep Jusufi?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. Does your name appear as "Zenep Jusofosa" on your passport, though?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Jusufi, is your ethnicity Albanian?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what is your husband's name?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Elmaz Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you presently reside in Ljuboten village, in the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: How long have you lived in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: For 42 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And were you residing in Ljuboten on 12 August 2001?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: On 12 August 2001, who lived with you at your residence in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Myself, my husband, my son, and the son of the uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And what is your son's name?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Rami Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: In the early morning hours, Ms. Jusufi, on 12 August 2001, were you at your home?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. He was at home, sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, my question was: Were you, Mrs. Jusufi, were you present at your home?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And around 5.00 in the morning on that date, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I took my husband to the yard just to take him out for fresh air. He's an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the Court's permission, because of Mrs. Jusufi's difficulty in manipulating or dealing with the technology that's in the courtroom, I'd like to, with the Court's permission, I'd like to show the exhibits I intend to tender with this witness in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, you mentioned you had a son Rami Jusufi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could ask for the usher's assistance in displaying on the ELMO a photograph which is 65 ter 609, page one, bearing ERN 05016269. It is also in the binders provided for this witness today, tab 3. Tab 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: It's Rami.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. So you're looking at the photograph that's being displayed in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: That's a photograph of your son Rami Jusufi?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you told us, Mrs. Jusufi, that you took your husband, Mr. Jusufi, to the yard on the 12th of August around 5.00 in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And when you were out in your yard, did you notice or hear anything outside of your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: There was a lot of noise, people talking. A lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And these people who were talking, did you recognise what language they were speaking in?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you understand the Macedonian language?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, just a few words. A little bit, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Did you see these people who you heard speaking?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Did you actually see them?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them with my eyes. The gate was locked, was closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Now, you're referring to a gate. If I may ask the usher's assistance once more to show Mrs. Jusufi 65 ter 199.3, which is also tab 6 of the binders provided today. It's bearing -- I'm sorry, tab 6. I'm sorry, it's tab 6. Thank you. This photograph bears N0057596. It's also photo C, page 9 of the official court binder. Mrs. Jusufi, do you see that photograph that's being displayed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's mine, it's ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me, what do you mean by "ours"? Can you tell me, what's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: It's our house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is it the yard area of the house that you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is the yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Is this the area where you and Mr. Jusufi were that morning on the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. That morning, we were here in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And by "here," do you mean the yard that's depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And if you could take a look at the photograph to the left -- I mean, sorry, to the right of the photograph, there is a blue wall or a blue gate there?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Is this the gate that --

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: That's the gate, the gate that takes you outside the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And this gate takes you outside the house. Where does it take you to; to a street?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, to the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And these voices that you heard that day on the 12th, were they out on the street or where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: From the street. They were going towards the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And later on that morning, did you go back outside to this area?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, I didn't. At 7.30, because the noise was growing bigger, I took my husband inside and started to prepare breakfast. Actually, we didn't even manage to eat our breakfast, because the war began. My son was asleep, and then the gate, the blue gate, was kicked open. And I told my son to wake up. He put on his clothes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, let me stop you there for a second. Okay? Let's go one step at a time for a minute. When you took your husband out to the yard and you heard these voices, at some point then did you take your husband back in the house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. I brought him inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is that when you said you tried to make breakfast?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And then after -- when you tried to make breakfast, did you -- you said you heard some noises again. What noises were those?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go outside again. I stayed inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear the people speaking again?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear them anymore. I was scared to go outside to the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: So when you went back inside to make breakfast for your husband, who was inside the house with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: My son, myself, my husband, then the son of our uncle who had come to have breakfast with us and coffee with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And do you know the son of the uncle that you mentioned, what is his name?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Muzafer Jusufi is his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: So once you get inside the house and you hear these noises, and you said you were afraid, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I stayed inside. What else could I do?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what did you see, if anything, happen after -- after that, after you heard the noises?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: When the war began, the door was kicked open. They killed my son at the door leading to the corridor. The house then was filled up with policemen and whatever they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: When you say they kicked the door, which door do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: The gate, the door to the yard. I don't know how they opened it, but there was this big burst. With grenades or something. That was this big noise that even that the windows were shaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And then when you say "the police," how do you know these people were the police?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: They were speaking Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see what these people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was behind the door, but my old man saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And by "old man" --

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: They had masks on their heads. I could only see some of them for a short moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- do you know how many of them you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, I didn't count them. I was too scared.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And where were you in the house when you saw these men?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: On the right side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: On the right side. Were you inside a room?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, inside a room.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could you see your front door from the inside of the room where you -- where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, you cannot see the gate, but there is another door on this side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. To assist you, perhaps we could show, with the usher's help, tab 5 of the binder that's been provided today, which is 65 ter 199.2. It's bearing ERN N0057595.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: It is also, for the Court, photo B, page 9, of the court binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, do you see the photograph that is being displayed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what is that photograph of?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Photograph of my house, the part that takes you inside my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is this the front area of the house that you were talking about earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the front side of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: So for clarification, your house has a gate, and also in this photograph it looks like there's a door to your house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. That's the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And you said at some point, Rami was -- was killed. Can you tell us what you saw -- well, let's go back for a second. When you and your husband went back to the house after hearing the noises in the yard, you go into the house and Rami is there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: What was Rami doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Sleeping, he was sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no need to object. Since the witness already answered the question, I have no reason to object.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what did you do -- when you went back in the house with your husband and Rami was sleeping, did you do anything to Rami at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: When I entered the house, as I said, I was going to prepare breakfast around that time. He was still sleeping, my son.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And then what did you do after you started to prepare breakfast?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I started to make breakfast, but the electricity went off. Many victims fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And after the electricity off -- went off, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: We stayed inside. There was nothing else we could do. I had a gas stove, so I started to prepare some tea on the gas stove.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And after that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I stayed inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. At some point, did Rami wake up?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: When the gate was opened, Rami woke up and went to the entrance door, trying to close it, to lock it. But as soon as he got to the door, they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And how did they kill him?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: They killed him, the army or whatever they were. He was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And by "wounded," do you know how he was wounded? Well, let me withdraw that. Do you -- Mrs. Jusufi, at some point when you saw Rami being killed, where were you in the house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I was inside, in the room to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could you see Rami from where you were inside?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, I could see Rami from where I was, because he was killed inside the house, in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And where was Rami when you saw him get killed?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: At the entrance door. He was trying to close the door. The door was wide open because it was summer, so he was trying to close the door. They saw him and they wounded him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Did you hear any noises at the time when you saw Rami get wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? Yes, I heard a lot of noise. They all entered the house. They were in the yard, many of them. I could hear noises. I could hear noises, but I could not understand. My -- my husband knows that better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: What kind of noises did you hear?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: They said something like, "There is an invalid there." This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And did you hear any other -- besides voices, did you hear any other noises?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you know what caused Rami's wounds?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: The police, the army, whoever they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: They were speaking Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, what did these people do to your son?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: They wounded him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you know how they wounded him?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I don't know from where they shot, what kind of weapon they fired, but he was hit by bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And after Rami was hit by bullets, did you see Rami?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He was there at the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what happened to Rami when you saw him get hit by bullets?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Was he still at the front door?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And were you still in the same position that you described to us earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. They came at the door, the entrance door. They kicked that open. They were firing towards the washing machine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. At some point, did the firing stop?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: After this was set on fire, we were covered in smoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And while you were in your house and you saw Rami get -- get hit by the officers, what I'm asking is, what did -- at some point, did the shooting that you heard stop?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Would you please repeat it? I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has never said that she has seen that Rami has been hit by some officers, as it is said at page 21, line 18. I would like to ask the Prosecution not to testify in the place of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Ms. Motoike.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: You said that they were firing towards the washing machine. At some point, did the firing stop?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. After this gas container was set on fire, a three- or four-litre gas container was set on fire as well. Then they went back, and we took our son and brought him inside in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: The gas container that you mentioned, where was that located?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: It was close to the phone, in the corridor, in the entrance area. Both the phone and the container were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And that was inside your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could ask for the usher's assistance again. If he could show tab 1 of the witness binder that was provided today, which is 65 ter number 608, page number 5, bearing ERN 05016263.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, I apologise. I have to show you this photograph. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. It's my son, Rami Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is this what Rami looked like that day you saw him after being hit by bullets?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher's permission to -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: After you moved Rami to the room inside your house, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I lost my consciousness. I wasn't aware any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what happened to Rami?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: You can see for yourselves. He died immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: At the time when you saw Rami going to the door, did you see any weapons in Rami's hands?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would like to object. We would object for some of the questions that the esteemed colleague is suggesting. They are leading questions. The last one being the one that she would like to hear the answer to is also a leading question. Before that, we did not want to intercept the -- we don't want to harm the matter of the dead Rami Jusufi, but we would like to ask not to have any more leading questions asked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I indicate I've not seen any real reason for concern at the questions that have been put so far. The last question directed to a subject matter but did not indicate at all what would be the answer or the preferred answer. An issue of some materiality in this case, I would anticipate from your reaction, is whether the dead lad was armed or not armed at the time he was shot. She asked that question in a way that did not suggest a particular answer, and in the context of this case that certainly would seem not to be a matter of objection. Carry on, please, Ms. Motoike.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, I'd asked you at the time when you saw Rami going to the door, did you see any weapons in Rami's hands?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any weapon in his hands. We never had weapons in our house. I myself don't know what weapons are. I have only seen them on TV. There have never been weapons in our house or in the village, in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: At some point on that day, the 12th of August, did you have -- after Rami was wounded, did you have an opportunity to go outside your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I couldn't even bring some water for my son. He wanted water, and I couldn't go out and get some water because they were on the terrace, shooting from our terrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Those who were firing, who were shooting, the police, those who did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And you referred to the police. Why do you say they were the police?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: What else could they have been? It was the police, those that they had collected and brought there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: How were these people dressed?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I didn't see them. My husband did, but I personally didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if this might be an appropriate time to break. I don't have much longer, but I know that the interpreters probably do need a break, so I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's too early yet, so unless there's a problem, another quarter of an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could ask for the usher's assistance once more. Could we please show Mrs. Jusufi tab 7 of the binder that's been provided today. It's 65 ter number 197, page 168, bearing ERN N0014925-08.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, do you see the photograph that's being displayed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: What is this a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And by the "house," do you mean your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And at some point on the 12th of August, after all of this happened and after they were on the terrace, did you have an occasion to go outside your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No. We stayed in the house for 12 hours. It was impossible for us to leave the house and go even in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: At some point, did you go to the yard after the 12 hours?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Darkness fell then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. On the next day, did you go outside of your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: What could we do on the next day?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: Did you step outside your house the next day?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: We left the house, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you see the photograph that's marked -- that's being displayed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And do you see the door in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what is that door?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: It's the entrance door from where you enter the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And can you tell us if this door depicted in the photograph, does it look like the door to your house as it is now?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: With the -- do you see that there's broken glass in the windows of the door?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: The glasses were all broken on the first and the second floor. Nothing was left intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And did the door look like it is in the photograph, with the broken glass? Did it look like that after the police arrived at your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And do you see the bottom part --

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: The police broke them. This, the car on fire, the house, everything we, had they set them on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you see the bottom part of the photograph, in the bottom right corner of the photograph? Do you recognise what's depicted in that part of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: They burned the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the photograph that's in front of you. In the bottom right corner of the photograph. Do you recognise the things in the bottom right of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I don't see anything here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps show her the actual hard copy? I have an additional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question might be directed to the bottom centre of the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I see them now. They are bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And did you see those on the day after the police arrived at your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These are the bullets that entered the house the day that they shot at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: You mentioned that the car was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could we please show Mrs. Jusufi tab 9 of the binder that's provided today, which is 65 ter 197, page 166, bearing ERN N0014925-05.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, do you see that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: It is the car that this -- that they burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And showing you, with the usher's assistance, tab 11 of the binder that's been provided today, 65 ter 197, page 173, bearing ERN N001492515.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, do you see the photograph that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I see the car and some burned materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And by "the car," do you mean the same car that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: This is the car. You are asking me about the car? Yeah, it is the same car, our car.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And this -- in the middle of the photograph, there looks to be what looks to be a gate. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: It is the gate -- the entrance gate, the yard gate which they shot at.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Did your gate look like this prior to the officers arriving at your residence that day?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, but it was good, in good condition. It was painted, and then they shelled it and brought it to this state. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That's all the questioning I have with respect to Mrs. Jusufi. However, I would ask to tender the photographs, that I've shown her, into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe you've not shown all the photographs. You intended that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: I intended not to show all of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could ensure, with the court officer during the break, exactly which numbers in the tab you propose to tender as an exhibit, and with that she can be ready to receive them after the break. In the meantime, could I just clarify one or two things, please, with you, Mrs. Jusufi? I'm sorry to take you back to this matter, but you mentioned that your son was shot as he was in your house, inside the front door, and you mentioned then that these people, who were speaking Macedonian, stepped back from the door, and you were able, as I understood you, to move your son into a room in the house. Was your son at that stage alive or dead? Are you able to help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am -- I can't understand it. I showed you once. I don't seem to remember everything. I forget things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can understand that. You did indicate at one stage that you weren't able to get water for your son. Did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He asked me for water. He was thirsty. But I don't seem to remember everything, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And when he asked you for water, that was after he'd been shot, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After they shot him, he asked for water. We couldn't provide him water, and then he died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I also noticed that in the photograph, a bandage had been put around his wounds, around his stomach. Do you know who put the bandage on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, because there was a lot of blood coming out of the wound. I tied the belly with a piece of sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And when you did that, was your son still alive or had he died by then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He died at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry to have had to ask you about those matters, Mrs. Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if 300 years passed by and I'm alive, I won't forget that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. What we will do now is have a break. We must have a break for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't have anything else to say. I think I told you everything, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but there will be a few more questions from other counsel. I hope you will be able to bear with us there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to hear any more questions because I don't have anything to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. We will have a break to enable you to refresh yourself, and then we'll resume here at a quarter past 4.00. We've got to do that because some of the tapes in the technology here must be changed after an hour and a half, and a half an hour is needed for that. So if you would be good enough, when we leave the courtroom, to go with the court officer to the room where you can rest for a little while, and then if you would return here when you're asked. Thank you very much, Mrs. Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Motoike, you wanted to tender certain exhibits, and you've discussed those with the court officer, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I would ask the court officer then to indicate the numbers assigned, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document under tab 3, and that is 65 ter 609, photograph 1, will become Exhibit P-1. The document under tab 6, 65 ter number 199.3 will become Exhibit P-2. The document under tab 5, 65 ter number 199.2, will become Exhibit P-3. The document under tab 1, 65 ter number 608, page 5, will become Exhibit P-4. The document under tab 7, 65 ter 197, page 168, will become Exhibit P-5. The document under tab 9, 65 ter 197, page 166, will become Exhibit P-6. And the document under tab 11, 65 ter 197, page 173, will become Exhibit P-7. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, does that conclude your examination, Ms. Motoike?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There will be some further questions now. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Ms. Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic, and together with my colleague, Guenal Mettraux, I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Ljube Boskoski. Before I start asking questions that I intend to ask you, I wish, on behalf of Mr. Boskoski and on behalf of his Defence counsels, to express my condolences for the loss of your son. Also, Mrs. Jusufi, I wish to thank you for the fact that more than a year ago, you admitted me into your house in Ljuboten, and you allowed me to have an interview with you and your husband about the event that you testified about before this court. I would like to ask you, Mrs. Jusufi, if you do not understand my question, please let me know immediately and I will repeat the question so that you are able to answer that question. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I have no more answers to give. I have nothing more to add. I already said what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Judge if he could clarify to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your question, please, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, you stated that you are the wife of Elmaz Jusufi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With Mr. Elmaz Jusufi, you've had four children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One of your sons has died several years ago, and the eldest son, Rami, was killed in the village on the 12th of August, 2001, as you have testified before this Court; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Jusufi, you have two children: your son Salahedin and your daughter, Peret [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the house that you have recognised in the photographs, you used to live in the year 2001 with your husband, who is disabled, and with your daughter -- son, Rami, his wife and children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak closer to the microphones, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The youngest son, Salahedin --

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Rami's wife with four children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So the wife of the killed Rami had four children with Rami, and they live with you now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, they live with us because they have nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your younger son, Mrs. Jusufi, Salahedin, used to live in his house adjacent to yours?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: In his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in his house. Salahedin lives in his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in the year 2001, your youngest son was married as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. My youngest son has been married for 12 years now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can go to the door of your son to a garden gate?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No, he has his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct? Your daughter, Miberan [phoen], is married and lives with her husband, Ismail Durmishi?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: She lives in Ljuboten, in the neighbourhood Durmisina. That is one kilometre away from your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could come to your daughter's house through the road, or via a meadow and a creek, behind which immediately on the right-hand side there is the house of your daughter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already stated to our colleague, the Prosecutor, that you live in the family house, and tell me, is it correct that your house is located in the vicinity of the Orthodox Church in Ljuboten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask now that the witness is shown court binder page 9, photograph number 65, 65 ter, number 199.2. This is the photograph that the Prosecutor has already shown to the witness, and it has been given the label "table 5". I apologise. I was just told that that photograph has been given the Prosecution number P-3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, can you indicate in this photograph the garden gate through which you could go to the house of your younger son?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: It was behind the house. It was burned. Can't see it here, I can't find it here. We have to go from the other side. There isn't any gate on our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So then in this photograph, you were not able to recognise the entrance in to the house of your son, because it is located behind your house and it can't be seen in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: There is, in front of our house, there is a road that comes round.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please help me now a bit, Mrs. Jusufi. Let's see how one arrives to your house. Is it correct that if, from Skopje, we're coming to Ljuboten, from the direction of the village of Ljubanci, then one must pass by the house of Brace and several Macedonian houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That street comes to a crossroad with the street 5, that is, the Main Street in Ljuboten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the very crossroad, there is a shop; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that shop to your house, you need to turn to the right towards the direction of the Orthodox Church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: On the left, yes, you turn on the left and our house is on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Around your house, there is a wall with a metal gate that prevents people seeing from the street what happens inside the court -- inside the garden of your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I didn't go out to look.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you have never viewed your house from the street; is that what you wish to say, Mrs. Jusufi?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I have gone out on the street, but I didn't pay attention, I didn't look whether you can see or not see inside my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mrs. Jusufi, that the majority of the houses in your neighbourhood also have walls that prevents a view from the main street inside the house and the gardens around the houses?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your neighbourhood --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you, Mrs. Jusufi, to repeat the answer, because it did not go into the transcript of the session. So is it correct that all houses in your neighbourhood have such walls around them?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, they do, and you cannot see into their yards. You can't see anything inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to ask now that the witness is shown Prosecution Exhibit P-2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, a while ago you indicated the front gate, the one painted blue, that separates your garden, your yard, from the main street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mrs. Jusufi, that when you go through that gate, your yard has a slight incline by which you climb down to your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you can see the house here. It's my son's house, but there is no garden gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mrs. Jusufi, I would like to ask now that you're shown 65 ter number 197 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask, since they can't be found on the e-court, I would like to ask that the witness is shown a photograph in the 65 ter list of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusufi, judging from the position of this car that you see in the photograph, is it completely clear that your yard, from the front gate, from the main street, has a slope -- a slight incline coming towards your house?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell me now, Mrs. Jusufi, is it correct that in your neighbourhood live the families Jusufi, then a bit further away from you the family of Kamberi, and the closest Macedonian neighbour is Sande Kostovski; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Kamberi family, namely, Fatmir Kamberi, has in your neighbourhood two houses: one is located in the small lane, Mal Sokak, and the other one is towards the mosque and the second one was burned. Are these facts correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that in your neighbourhood predominantly the Jusufi families are living, could you, Mrs. Jusufi, tell the Court whether it is correct that in Ljuboten, as in most Albanian villages, in the neighbourhood there are mainly families living, families that are related by blood?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, seven or eight households are related by kin. We're all Jusufis. My husband knows these things better.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those families, as is customary in Ljuboten as well, are related by blood through the male stream; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The women are marrying and going to the family and the neighbourhood of their husband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And so your daughter got married and went to live in the neighbourhood Durmisina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago, Mrs. Jusufi, we discussed the wall that surrounds the yard of your house and other houses. Tell me, please, is that also part of the tradition in the Albanian community which aims to preserve the privacy of each of the families from the unnecessary interference from other people into their family life. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, if we're discussing the tradition of your people, can we say that a husband within a family, in the Albanian people, in the Albanian community, has the main say, and the woman respects what the husband says and does not contradict this? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, especially in the rural regions, many of the women do not decide to go to school or they terminate their schooling very early; is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Who is willing to, they continue with their schooling, and who is not, they stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the tradition of the Albanian people, the men are the ones who preserve the honour of the family, especially of the mother and the wife and the daughter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it correct that the men in the family have the duty to say -- to guard the honour and the respect of the mother and daughter?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, briefly about some general issues. Tell me, is it correct that in the tradition of the Albanian people, a word, once given, the so-called besa, a promise, must not be broken?

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Persons -- I apologise, the answer was not "no." I will repeat the question. Is it correct, Mrs. Jusufi --

utterances.speaker: ZENEP JUSUFI
utterances.text: I didn't hear you quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that in the tradition of the Albanian people, and also in your village, Ljuboten, people, when they make a besa, a promise, that besa must be respected?
